list.listitem: Diagnose early to prevent maternal and infant morbidity; offer dietary counseling, ginger, vitamin B6, and doxylamine to women presenting with protracted nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (NVP). A
Many antiemetic medications are safe in pregnancy and can help with treatment of NV, but their efficacy is limited in true hyperemesis gravidarum (HG). B
A trial of oral or IV steroids may be warranted in women who do not respond to other medications. B
Adjunctive treatment with acupressure, and possibly acupuncture, can be helpful to some women and does not increase morbidity. B
Hospitalization, IV fluid hydration, and possibly parenteral nutrition should be considered in the most severely-ill patients. C

background.definition: Hyperemesis gravidarum (HG) is a severe form of nausea and vomiting of pregnancy (NVP), characterized by persistent vomiting, dehydration, ketosis, electrolyte disturbances, and loss of more than 5% of prepregnancy body weight. Caution is advised in interpreting published literature as authors of a systematic review found 11 definition items of HG among 31 published trials.

list.listitem: 0.3 to 2% (approximately 1 in 200 pregnancies).

In a population-based cohort study in England of over 8 million pregnancies, hospitalizations for HG occurred in 121,885 pregnancies or 1.48%. In this study, younger age, lower socioeconomic status, being of Asian or Black race, carrying a female fetus and having a multiple pregnancy, in addition to certain comorbidities noted below, significantly increased HG and readmission risk; only ethnicity increased reoccurrence risk.

An incidence of 1.3% was reported for hospitalization for HG in a 2005-2017 population-based cohort study in Finland. Compared with control women with no history of HG, cases were of younger maternal age, higher gravidity, and more likely to be underweight or overweight. Other risk factors were assisted reproductive technology, multiple gestation and female sex of the fetus. Compared to case-women’s non-HG pregnancies, higher age and obesity were associated with higher risk of hyperemesis. Smoking was associated with lower risk.
In contrast, NVP occurs in up to 70% of pregnancies.

Based on a population-based cohort using medical records of 417,028 pregnancies from 1998-2014, the overall prevalence of clinically-recorded NVP/HG was 9.1%. Hospital admission occurred in 2.1%, and 3.4% were treated with antiemetics in primary care only.

Patients experience significant emotional distress; in one study of 209 women with HG, almost half met criteria for both anxiety and depression. In another study of 200 women with HG, there was a 76-fold increase in the risk of depression. Authors of a systematic review of 12 studies confirmed higher rates of depression and anxiety in women with HG. There appears to be a reassuring pattern of rebound from depression, anxiety and stress in women with HG by the third trimester of pregnancy.

Maternal adverse outcomes include sequelae of malnutrition such as poor wound healing and immunosuppression; rare complications can include Wernicke encephalopathy from untreated vitamin B1 deficiency, Mallory-Weiss tears, esophageal rupture, splenic avulsion, acute kidney injury, and pneumothorax.
Fetal adverse outcomes include low birth weight, growth restriction, and prematurity.
Idiopathic.

Possible causes include hormones [elevated HCG and/or progesterone, decreased thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)], delayed gastric motility, chronic Helicobacter (H.) pylori infection, and psychological factors. There are genetic predisposing factors as well.

A meta-analysis identified 31 studies including 5852 pregnant patients who were H. pylori infection positive and 8196 pregnant patients who were H. pylori negative. Those who were positive for H. pylori had a 14-fold-higher odds of having HG (OR 14.5, 95% CI 10.2-20.4).
Based on genome-wide association data from the FinnGen cohort and UK Biobanks, 11 genetic variants were associated with HG.
Among 40 women with HG, there was a correlation between increased levels of depression and anxiety and increased salivary levels of cortisol and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate.
Women with HG also have significantly higher serotonin levels than women with or without morning sickness.
Unknown.

In a case-control study, serum levels of cachexia genes GDF15 and IGFBP7 were significantly increased in women with HG at 12 weeks' gestation compared to control women with or without NVP. At 24 weeks gestation, when symptoms had largely resolved, there were no differences in GDF15 and IGFBP7 serum levels between cases and controls.
Infant morbidity is primarily the result of maternal malnutrition, nutrient deficiency, and inadequate weight gain.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: History of migraine or motion sickness
Clinical diagnosis H. pylori with confirmatory testing

list.listitem: Taking a multivitamin at the time of conception may decrease the incidence of HG.A
The United States Preventive Services Task Force does not offer any screening guidelines regarding HG. C
HG is primarily a clinical diagnosis. Loss of more than 5% of prepregnancy weight and ketonuria unexplained by other causes are indicative of the condition. C

Obtain an electrolyte panel to evaluate for derangements like hypokalemia or metabolic acidosis, CBC to evaluate for hemoconcentration due to volume contraction, urine for ketones, specific gravity or the evidence of an infection, and TSH and T4 to evaluate for hyperthyroidism. C
Consider ultrasound to rule out multiple gestation or hydatidiform mole. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Presence of ophthalmopathy, goiter, or signs of hyperthyroidism
Limited duration of illness; presence of diarrhea
Lower severity of illness; absence of weight loss or electrolyte disturbances
Abnormalities on neurologic testing, such as vertigo or nystagmus
History of previous disease, or abnormalities on psychiatric evaluation

list.listitem: Assess weight compared with prepregnancy weight; if more than 5% loss, consider HG as a diagnosis.
Assess hydration status by examining skin turgor and moisture of mucous membranes.

Use of the Pregnancy Unique Quantification of Emesis and nausea (PUQE score) instrument is a severity measure endorsed by the 2022 expert guideline from the College of French Gynecologists and Obstetricians. They suggest that a score of ≥7 can be used to distinguish HG and a score of ≥13 suggests a need for inpatient treatment.
Laboratory tests: CBC, electrolytes, TSH, T4, LFTs (liver function tests), urinalysis, renal function tests (BUN/creatinine) in all pregnant women with intractable vomiting.
Although ketonuria is often used as a defining feature of HG, there is no association between ketonuria and the presence or severity of HG based on 5 studies.
Perform more specific laboratory testing as indicated by clinical presentation.
Obtain obstetrical ultrasound to exclude multiple gestation or molar pregnancy.
Liver biopsy is generally not indicated even in the presence of abnormal LFTs.

In a retrospective study of 73 women with severe HG, there was a significant increase in the level of hCG compared to age- and gestational age-matched women without hyperemesis; this may alter the results of the triple test screen.
Please see for a suggested approach to management.
Supportive care, along with counseling on dietary modification and trigger avoidance, is the mainstay of treatment. C

Consider a trial of oral ginger or Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine), alone or with doxylamine 25 mg daily, early during the illness. A The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologist (ACOG) consider vitamin B6 with or without doxylamine to be first-line therapy. A Cochrane review, however, found limited data supporting vitamin B6, doxylamine‐pyridoxine and other anti‐emetic drugs to relieve mild or moderate NV in early pregnancy.

In more severe disease, a trial of antiemetics such as ondansetron, promethazine, or metoclopramide is appropriate; however, efficacy is limited in true HG.The drugs are likely equally effective but may differ in side effects, and supporting data are few, with no clear differences shown between drugs.B

IV fluid replacement and parenteral nutrition may be necessary in the most severely-ill patients. Add thiamine 100 mg IV daily for 3 days if vomiting has persisted for more than 3 weeks to prevent Gayet-Wernicke encephalopathy. C
Oral or IV steroids can be considered in patients who are unresponsive to other treatments. B

listitem.strong: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) with or without doxylamine

list.listitem: Vitamin B6 25 mg thrice daily or the combination of B6 and doxylamine is safe and effective in some women for NV in early pregnancy and is first-line therapy. Authors of a systematic review confirmed effectiveness of pyridoxine for mild symptoms.

In an RCT with 60 women at high risk of recurrence of severe NVP, use of preemptive pyridoxine-doxylamine combination reduced recurrence of moderate-severe symptoms compared with treatment once symptoms begin (15.4% vs 39.1%).

Addition of vitamin B6 to either metoclopramide or prochlorperazine was more effective than either monotherapy alone in one RCT of 174 women with first trimester NV. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved a combination preparation of doxylamine succinate 10 mg/pyridoxine hydrochloride 10 mg (Diclegis) in 2013.

In an RCT of 92 women hospitalized with HG there was no benefit of vitamin B6 in conjunction with metoclopramide on rehospitalization rate, vomiting frequency, or nausea score. Cochrane authors also found no benefit of vitamin B6 for HG.

Two double-blinded RCTs showed benefit of a short course of oral or IV steroids; these can be tried if other interventions are unsuccessful.However, authors of a meta-analysis of 5 trials found no effect of corticosteroids on readmission rates; single small trials supported a reduction of vomiting episodes and improved well-being but none reported on perinatal outcomes.
Authors of one meta-analysis of HG treatment concluded unclear benefit from corticosteroids and recommended consideration as a third-line agent in severe cases.

However, in a more recent meta-analysis of 18 treatment studies of HG, authors found an OR of 6.7 (95% CI 1.1 to 38.8) supporting methylprednisolone for better control of HG symptoms compared to standard care based on very-low quality evidence.

Antihistamine H1 receptor blockers, phenothiazines, selective 5-HT3 receptor antagonists and benzamide are effective for reducing NV in early pregnancy, but have limited efficacy in treating HG. In one before and after case series of women with HG, the combination of metoclopramide and diphenhydramine was somewhat better than droperidol and diphenhydramine in improving vomiting symptoms (36% vs. 21%) with comparable length of hospitalization (3.7 vs. 3.1 days) and rate of rehospitalization for HG (19.2% vs. 24.4%).
In one RCT, investigators found similar benefit for metoclopramide and promethazine, but a better side-effect profile for metoclopramide, resulting in less discontinuation of the drug.
Authors of a Cochrane review found limited data supporting superiority of one agent over another for symptomatic relief in HG.

Data regarding ondansetron are conflicting. Ondansetron was found to be more effective than pyridoxine/doxylamine combination therapy with a NNT of 2 (95% CI 1.4-5.9) for nausea and NNT of 2.4 (95% CI 1.5-17.4) for vomiting. Authors of a meta-analysis found ondansetron reduced hospital length of stay in patients with HG (weighted mean difference -0.2, 95% CI -0.31 to -0.01).

A 14-day course of ondansetron resulted in significantly decreased NV compared to metoclopramide in another study. However, the most recent RCT demonstrated equal efficacy for metoclopramide and ondansetron for hyperemesis; drowsiness and dry mouth were more frequent for metoclopramide. Intestinal obstruction has been reported in association with use of ondansetron for HG.

There is uncertainty about an association between ondansetron use and congenital anomalies. In a recent report of first trimester exposure to intravenous or oral ondansetron, which occurred in 11% of 33,677 deliveries at a single institution in Pennsylvania over 9 years, there was a dose-dependent increased risk of ventral septal defects with OR ranging from 1.7 to 3.2 (1.0-9.9) for the highest dose exposure.
Transdermal clonidine was shown beneficial compared to placebo for symptom control in a pilot study of women with severe HG.
Diazepam was found in a meta-analysis to reduce risk of hospital admission for HG (OR 0.11, 95% CI 0.01-0.95) based on very low-quality evidence.
Gabapentin was more effective than standard-of-care therapy for reducing nausea and vomiting and increasing global satisfaction in outpatients with HG in an RCT of 21 patients.
With respect to rehydration fluids, 5% dextrose with 0.9% saline and 0.9% saline alone appear comparable.

In a retrospective review of 33 women with HG, use of a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) line during care resulted in a high rate of infection and/or thromboembolism, with 22 requiring treatment; the authors recommend against use of PICC lines for these patients. ACOG recommends against routine insertion of PICC lines due to the significant complications associated with them.

A placebo-controlled, double-blinded RCT showed benefit of ginger 250 mg taken before meals and at bedtime (total 1 g per day). Cochrane authors found 3 recent studies supporting ginger over placebo for early NVP, but evidence of effectiveness was limited and inconsistent. Authors of a 2016 systematic review also concluded that ginger was effective for treating mild symptoms.

Evidence supports the effectiveness of acupuncture or pericardium 6 (p6) acupressure.In a RCT of 120 hospitalized women with HG, use of an acupressure band at P6 for 12 hours daily for three days vs. a sham band significantly reduced the symptoms of NV, retching and ketonuria and led to a reduction in hospital stay of 1 day (average 2.88 vs. 3.88 days, respectively). A similar reduction in nausea and vomiting was reported in another RCT of 90 hospitalized patients with HG comparing an acupressure wristband at the P6 point three times daily compared to regular doses of intravenous antiemetics.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 18 studies found that acupuncture (OR 18.9, 95% CI 2.1-168) and acupressure (OR 26.7, 95% CI 2.5 to 283.1) were associated with better control of HG symptoms than standard care. Acupressure also decreased the need for rescue antiemetics (OR 0.06, 95% CI 0.01-0.44).

It is unclear whether electrostimulation of acupressure points is beneficial. Authors of a meta-analysis of 20 studies found a reduction for the combined outcome for NVP or HG in pregnancy as a dichotomous variable but no benefit when using continuous outcome measures for NV and the combined outcome.

Studies of hypnosis for HG are encouraging but study quality is poor. In a recent RCT including 41 patients hospitalized with HG, those randomized to 2 sessions of adjuvant hypnotherapy and instruction in daily self-hypnosis practice plus standard therapy had reduced severity of nausea and frequency of vomiting, and shorter hospital stay compared to compared to standard therapy alone.
The 2022 French guideline suggest stopping prenatal vitamins and iron supplementation without stopping folic acid supplementation. Diet and lifestyle should be adjusted according to symptoms.
Early enteral tube feeding for up to 7 days did not result in improved birth weight or secondary outcomes in one RCT of 116 women hospitalized for HG.

In an RCT of 160 women hospitalized with HG in Malaysia, there were no differences in satisfaction scores or 24-hour vomiting episodes between initial 12-hour fasting and immediate oral feeding, and women preferred the latter for future hospitalizations.

Patients who have suppressed TSH levels should not be treated for hyperthyroidism unless they have clear evidence of intrinsic thyroid disease, that is, antithyroid antibodies or goiter. In a case series of 143 women with HG, gestational transient thyrotoxicosis (GTT) was present in almost half and resolved by the second trimester in the 34 women who were followed biochemically. Both incidence and clinical vs. subclinical presence of GTT was related to serum hCG levels.

Offer the patient supportive psychotherapy and monitor for evidence of clinical depression. In one RCT of 86 women with HG, use of psychotherapy with 8 sessions over 3 weeks, in addition to vitamin B6, was superior to vitamin B6 alone for improved symptoms (Rhodes score).

Consider hospitalization in patients with continuing weight loss, significant orthostasis, or profound electrolyte disturbances—particularly severe hyponatremia or hypokalemia, that require carefully monitored replacement.

The French 2022 guideline suggests hospitalization when there is one or more of the following: weight loss ≥10%, one or more clinical signs of dehydration, PUQE score ≥13, hypokalemia <3.0mmol/L, hyponatremia <120mmol/L, elevated serum creatinine >100μmol/L or resistance to treatment.

Refeeding syndrome refers to a severe electrolyte disturbance (e.g., low serum concentrations of phosphate, magnesium, and potassium) and metabolic abnormalities in undernourished patients undergoing refeeding, regardless of route; it can be fatal.

Fetal death at 16-weeks gestation was reported in a 32-year-old woman with HG following admission for suspected refeeding syndrome after ingesting a sugar-rich beverage. In another case report, appetite recovery following HG was associated with simultaneous onset of rhabdomyolysis and diabetes insipidus due to electrolyte abnormalities.
Symptoms resolve by 16 to 18 weeks' gestation in 80% to 85% of women. C

In a systematic review, there was an increased risk of preterm delivery, low-birth-weight, and infant with a low 5-min Apgar score in pregnancy complicated by severe HG. Another systematic review showed an increased risk of lower birth weight and shorter gestational age, but did not show increased risk of low Apgar scores, congenital anomalies, or perinatal death. B
Women who catch up on weight gain (at least 7 kg) later in pregnancy are less likely to have a low-birth-weight or small for gestational-age infant. B
There is no clear increased risk of birth defects in offspring of women with HG. B

Authors of a systematic review including 19 studies found HG associated with small increases in adverse health outcomes among children. C These included anxiety disorder (OR 1.74, 95% CI 1.04-2.91), sleep problems (OR 2.94, 95% CI 1.25-6.93) and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and autism spectrum disorder. Evidence is based on few studies of low quality.

Women who develop hyperemesis in the second trimester of pregnancy have a 2-fold increased risk of preeclampsia, 3-fold increased risk of placental abruption, and a small increased risk of a small-for-gestational-age infant (OR 1.39; 95% CI 1.06-1.83).
Recurrence risk of HG is estimated at 15% to 81% based on a systematic review of five heterogeneous, low-quality studies with 40,350 HG cases.
Based on a Danish population cohort, women with HG have an increased risk of autoimmune disease (RR 1.41; 95% CI 1.3-1.51).
In a follow-up study completed by 72 of 215 participants previously admitted with HG, at an average of 4.5 years later, 39.7% met criteria for anxiety, 27.4% for depression, and 21.9% for PTSD.
Patients should make dietary changes to include eating smaller, more frequent meals, which are high in carbohydrates and low in fat.

Salty foods are often better tolerated in the morning and tart liquids (e.g., lemonade or electrolyte replacement drinks) may be better tolerated than water alone. Among 4 different food groups tested for tolerability in 72 hospitalized patients with HG, sweet apple had the highest agreeability score and lowest nausea severity and intolerance-emesis response rate of 4% followed by watermelon (10%), crackers (11%) and white bread (17%).
Medical staff and family members should provide emotional support to the patient as HG can result in depression and other affective changes.

cell.label: Suspect HG in pregnant woman with intractable vomiting, onset at <10 weeks' gestation, and >5% weight loss compared with prepregnancy weight.
Check electrolytes, urinalysis, TSH/T4, LFTs, BUN/creatinine; obtain ultrasound to assess for multiple gestation and molar pregnancy.
Offer ginger, vitamin B6, doxylamine, p6 acupressure.
Treat with antiemetics, IV fluid hydration, and electrolyte replacement; consider steroids.
Consider hospitalization, total parenteral nutrition (TPN), specialist consultation.
Treat any underlying disease or abnormalities.
